summary: Describes how the Path Computation Element architecture can be applied to determining a sequence of domains for Label Switched Paths across multiple domains in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks. No single point knows all links and resources in each domain, which causes the problem. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how cooperating path-computation elements could find a route across domains when the domain sequence is not known in advance. A parent planner chooses candidate domain routes while child planners keep their own internal topology information.

questions: what is the difference between brpc and hierarchical pce
subtitle: A hierarchical PCE framework for selecting domains and paths for inter-domain MPLS and GMPLS LSPs.

tldr.problem: Existing inter-domain path-computation methods assume the domain sequence is already known, while no single computation point sees every domain's topology and resources.
tldr.mechanism: A parent PCE keeps an abstract map of domain connectivity and coordinates child PCEs, which compute path segments within their own domains.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes a framework and requirements for future PCEP work. It is aimed at small groups of domains, not the whole Internet.

today: RFC 6805 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo does not specify protocol extensions.

sections.title: The Unknown Domain Sequence
sections.content:
Inter-domain MPLS and GMPLS path computation is difficult because no single point knows all links and resources in every domain. Existing per-domain and backward-recursive methods assume that the sequence of domains is known ahead of time.

This memo considers how to choose that sequence as part of finding an end-to-end path. Its goal is to support scalable computation while preserving domain confidentiality and avoiding the exchange of full traffic-engineering topology. The framework is intended for small groups of domains with limited ingress visibility, not a group as large as the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain knows its own roads, but no one may know which domains make the best complete route. The framework adds a way to choose that sequence without sharing every internal detail.

sections.title: Existing Computation Methods
sections.content:
With per-domain computation, the entry boundary node of each domain computes a path segment during signaling. A locally best segment can lead to a poor choice in the next domain, so the complete path may be suboptimal. This method can suit simply connected domains with known preferred interconnections.

Backward-Recursive PCE-based Computation (BRPC) coordinates PCEs along a known domain sequence. The egress PCE starts a tree of candidate paths, and each PCE toward the ingress adds its own domain paths. The ingress PCE then selects the complete path. Extending this to an unknown sequence by sending information to every neighboring domain would create path-computation flooding and scaling concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing one domain segment at a time can make a poor overall route. Asking every reachable domain for options may find better routes but can create too much computation and messaging.

sections.title: Parent and Child PCEs
sections.content:
The parent PCE maintains a map where child domains and their interconnections appear as a topology. It knows how domains connect and may know the traffic-engineering properties of those interconnections, but it does not know the internal topology or resource availability of child domains.

Each child PCE computes paths across its own domain and knows the identities of neighboring domains, not their internal topology. For a multi-domain request, the parent selects candidate domain sequences, asks relevant child PCEs for path segments, and combines their results under the requested objectives and local policies. The framework allows parent and child functions to be implemented in one PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent planner knows which domains connect. Each child planner knows roads inside its own domain and returns a path segment when asked.

sections.title: Objectives, Information, and Errors
sections.content:
An objective function defines what counts as a good path, such as minimizing cost, minimizing load, maximizing residual bandwidth, limiting the domains crossed, or preventing domain re-entry. The objective can be supplied by the requesting client, the ingress PCE under local policy, or the parent PCE under inter-domain policy.

Child PCEs are generally configured with their parent; parent-child discovery is outside the architecture. A parent may learn inter-domain connectivity from configuration or reports from child PCEs. If a child cannot find a path, the parent may cancel the request, relax constraints, or try another candidate domain. A child may replace a private path segment with a path-key to conceal its details.
sections.plainLanguage: The planners need a shared definition of a good route and a limited map of domain connections. If a path segment fails, the parent can try another route or adjust the request.

sections.title: Applicability, Management, and Security
sections.content:
The memo discusses applying hierarchical PCE to IGP areas, Autonomous Systems, and the ASON architecture. It also notes that BGP-TE information exchange makes different assumptions and could provide information to a PCE's traffic-engineering database.

Management must control which child PCEs can communicate with a parent and what information is shared. The framework aims to keep domain contents confidential, but the document notes that path segments can reveal topology or resource information and describes path-keys as one way to hide segment details. It does not define protocol extensions; it lists requirements for future PCEP work.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework is meant to protect each domain's internal map while still letting the parent choose a route. Administrators control which child planners connect and what information they report.
